evidence.text: While cholesterol modification enables an effective path to cell-enriched delivery, several limitations should be acknowledged.

The modification of the cholesterol headgroup with hydrophilic ligands, such as mannose, led to reduced encapsulation efficiency due to the steric hindrance introduced by the ligand, potentially limiting overall delivery efficiency.
Future studies will focus on optimizing formulation strategies to balance targeting specificity with efficient delivery.
Nonetheless, ligand-conjugated cholesterol introduces a new direction to preparing active-targeted LNPs.

evidence.text: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are an efficient and biocompatible platform for delivering genetic drugs that overcome various extracellular and intracellular barriers.1 They are typically composed of four molecules: ionizable amino lipids, cholesterol, phospholipids, and poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) lipids, that self-assemble with negatively charged nucleic acids to form discrete spheres capable of cellular uptake and endosomal escape.2 Because LNPs can transfect liver hepatocytes after intravenous administration,3-5 this approach has garnered clinical success in siRNA silencing6 and Cas9 mRNA/sgRNA CRISPR/Cas gene knockout7 of transthyretin to treat hereditary transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis.
Aspects of liver physiology and adsorption of apolipoprotein E (ApoE) to LNP surfaces8 has facilitated the delivery of mRNA and genome editors for therapeutic gene editing in hepatocytes.
evidence.context_after: However, to treat diseases in other cell types, approaches to enrich delivery to specific liver cells, other than hepatocytes, are an important goal.

evidence.text: While previous works have primarily focused on active targeting through the modification of PEG lipids and ionizable lipids, cholesterol presents an underexplored opportunity for functionalization to achieve cell-type-enriched delivery.
evidence.context_after: Cholesterol typically comprises about half of all LNP molecules due to beneficial effects on structural integrity, fluidity, and colloidal stability.21 Cholesterol has also been shown to affect LNP liver biodistribution, where a decrease in cholesterol in the LNP formulation can alter biodistribution and increase delivery to the lungs.22 Additionally, cholesterol is present on the outer surface of LNPs, and exposure to ApoE induces the migration of cholesterol from the core to the surface of the LNP.23,24 These studies describing the localization of cholesterol and ionizable amino lipids near the surface of LNPs following dePEGylation further support the feasibility to functionalize lipids for active targeting.

evidence.text: The surface of LNPs has been functionalized through the conjugation of ligands onto one or more lipid components.
Prefunctionalization involves first conjugating the desired ligand to a specific lipid, followed by the incorporation of the lipid–ligand conjugate into the LNP.
evidence.context_after: This strategy offers a simpler and more efficient process than postinsertion, in which lipid-conjugated ligands are introduced subsequent to LNP formulation.16 Moreover, this strategy enables control over the density of ligands on the surface of the LNP, thereby ensuring a higher degree of uniformity in lipid–ligand conjugates across each LNP.17 The most common prefunctionalization methodology consists of modifying the distal end of the PEG chain on the PEG lipid, as this site is most highly exposed and accessible on the LNP surface.18 For example, a mannose-functionalized PEG lipid was incorporated into LNPs, achieving the selective delivery of mRNA and siRNA to LSECs via mannose–CD206 interactions.19 Active targeting modification has also been performed on ionizable lipids.

LNPs have emerged as a powerful delivery system for RNA therapeutics in the liver, but the high accumulation in hepatocytes due to ApoE-dependent cellular uptake remains a significant challenge.

evidence.text: The liver consists of multiple cell types, including hepatocytes, liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs), Kupffer cells, dendritic cells, and stellate cells.9 Due to the propensity of LNPs to bind ApoE and utilize the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDL-R), achieving extrahepatic delivery may be enabled by active targeting strategies.10 Active targeting introduces the biofunctionalization of the LNP surface with ligands that specifically bind to cognate receptors expressed in target cells and induce receptor-mediated endocytosis.11,12 The surface can be modified with various types of ligands, including antibodies, proteins, peptides, small-molecule drugs, and carbohydrates.13,14 If LNPs can more effectively accumulate in target cells, the therapeutic index will be broader with reduced systemic toxicity.15

Lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery of mRNA to specific cell types is a necessary task for the development of safe and effective medicines.

LNP delivery to the liver is largely driven by the binding of serum ApoE to the LNP surface, followed by subsequent uptake in LDL receptor (LDL-R)-expressing hepatocytes, thereby reducing their utility in nonhepatocyte liver diseases.
Herein, we developed an active targeting strategy to overcome this limitation by incorporating mannose-conjugated cholesterol into LNPs.
evidence.context_after: Since cholesterol comprises about half of all molecules in LNPs, we reasoned that it could serve as a scaffold for active targeting.

evidence.context_before: With a series of ManCs in hand, we investigated the potential to formulate self-assembled mRNA LNPs containing ManC1–ManC5.
evidence.context_after: The base LNP formulation to examine the effect of adding a mannose-conjugated cholesterol consisted of the ionizable amino lipid 4A3–SC7, DOPE, cholesterol, and DMG–PEG2000 with a molar percentage of 23.8/23.8/47.6/4.8, which has previously been shown to effectively deliver mRNA to the liver.40-42 Lipid mix solutions in ethanol and nucleic acid in citrate buffer were mixed rapidly using the vortex method to formulate mannose-modified LNPs (Figure 3A).42 To test the maximal inclusion of mannose without hindering particle formation, we formed five different series of LNPs by increasing the percentage of ManC lipid from 0% to 100% of the total cholesterol content in 25% increments (Figure 3B).
